title: Patient-Reported Quality of Life and Functional Impairment in Liver Cirrhosis: Clinical Determinants from a Cross-Sectional Study
content: Background: Alcohol-related liver cirrhosis imposes a substantial clinical, functional, and psychosocial burden, significantly affecting patients' health-related quality of life (HRQoL). The aim of this study was to evaluate the relationship between disease severity, functional status, and HRQoL in patients with alcohol-related liver cirrhosis. Methods: This cross-sectional observational study included 144 adult patients with alcohol-related liver cirrhosis. Clinical, demographic, and laboratory data were collected, while HRQoL was assessed using the Short Form Liver Disease Quality of Life (SF-LDQOL) questionnaire. Disease severity was evaluated according to the Child–Pugh classification. Statistical analysis included descriptive statistics, Spearman correlation, the Kruskal–Wallis test, and multivariable logistic regression. Results: Most patients were classified as Child–Pugh A (75.7%), followed by Child–Pugh B (17.4%) and Child–Pugh C (6.9%). HRQoL was predominantly rated as fair or poor. Greater liver-related symptom burden and limitations in daily activities were significantly associated with poorer HRQoL. Patients with more advanced liver disease reported significantly lower HRQoL scores (p = 0.02), although impaired HRQoL was also observed in a substantial proportion of patients with compensated cirrhosis. In the multivariable analysis, social isolation remained independently associated with impaired overall HRQoL after adjustment for demographic and clinical characteristics. Conclusions: Health-related quality of life in patients with alcohol-related liver cirrhosis is influenced not only by disease severity but also by functional and psychosocial factors. Integrating patient-reported outcome measures with conventional clinical assessment may provide a more comprehensive evaluation of disease burden and support individualized multidisciplinary patient management.
